Reading

The innocent reading first. Asked for 'Books3', a name that is first the dataset's, the Overview gives the dataset: what it holds, who made it, which models it trained, and the suits and takedowns it drew, and offers at the end to show how to check whether a given author or title is in it.

Findings
  • THE DATASET IN THE TOOL'S PLACE. The census entity is The Atlantic's search tool, its address an article whose path is dated September 2023 and whose page returned 'Your access has been blocked'; the census row keeps 'three objects apart: the Books3 collection ..., the search tool named for it, and The Atlantic's reporting that carries the tool'. The query was the collection's name, and the composition answers about the collection. The tool enters twice: as the first card, 'AI Watchdog: Books3 - The Atlantic', a title other than the dated article the census row holds, and as the closing offer, 'how to check if a specific author or book title was included', the function a search tool over the collection would serve, which the composition offers without naming any tool.
  • THE COLLECTION AGAINST THE ONE SAVED ACCOUNT. Wikipedia's article on the Pile, the census row's only quoted source: 'The Books3 component of the dataset contains copyrighted material compiled from Bibliotik, a piracy website.', 'Books3 108.40' (GB), 'In July 2023, the Danish anti-piracy group Rights Alliance took down Books3 through DMCA notices.' The composition: 'scraped the files from shadow libraries', 'Rights groups issued DMCA notices, leading to the removal of components of the dataset from major hosting platforms like Hugging Face and The-Eye.' Bibliotik, the Rights Alliance and July 2023 are not named; the size is given in books, 'roughly 191,000 to 197,000', a range drawn from two cards ('>191,000' at The Atlantic, '197,000 downloaded ebooks' at the Substack), and the 108.40 GB is not given.
  • THE MAKER AND THE AUTHORS FROM SOURCES THE CENSUS DID NOT SAVE. 'Created in October 2020 by independent AI developer Shawn Presser' (the WIRED card: 'Shawn Presser created Books3 in October 2020 by scraping ~196,000 pirated books from a shadow library'); 'authors (such as Margaret Atwood, Stephen King, and Sarah Silverman) never consented or received compensation'. No saved source names Presser or any author in the collection; the Wikipedia article gives the 2024 suit as one 'filed in 2024 by three authors' and names none. The composition's suits target 'Meta, Bloomberg, and Adobe'.
  • THE PAGE THE CENSUS COULD NOT READ. The census row's Wikipedia source for Books3 itself returned 'Wikipedia does not have an article with this exact name.'; the composition's fifth card is the Pile's article ('Dataset: The Pile (886.03 GB, open-source, English text) created by EleutherAI, released December 31, 2020'), the census's one account of the collection. Whether The Atlantic's search still runs, which the census row's lifecycle leaves unrecorded, the composition does not say.
Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

At the collection's name the composition gives the collection, at a grain the census's one saved account does not reach, and leaves the search tool to a card and a closing offer. The census's separation of collection, tool and reporting is not drawn.

[QUERENT] Books3 [SYSTEM] Books3 is a controversial open-source text dataset containing over 191,000 pirated copyrighted books used widely to train generative artificial intelligence models. [[1], [2], [3]] Overview & Creation * What it is: A collection of roughly 191,000 to 197,000 digital fiction and nonfiction e-books (many with verified ISBNs). [[1], [2]] * Origin: Created in October 2020 by independent AI developer Shawn Presser, who scraped the files from shadow libraries to help democratize open-source large language model (LLM) training data. [[1], [2]] * The Pile: EleutherAI incorporated Books3 into The Pile, a massive 800GB+ open-source dataset released in late 2020 to train LLMs. [[1], [2], [3]] AI Usage & Industry Impact * Adopted by tech giants: Books3 has been utilized or referenced in the training data for models from major companies and organizations—including Meta (LLaMA), Bloomberg, Nvidia, Apple, and Anthropic. [[1], [2]] * Alternative datasets: Developers looking for clean or legal training data often turn to open alternatives like Project Gutenberg, Dolma, or EleutherAI's later ethically curated Common Pile release. [[1], [2]] Controversies & Legal Battles * Copyright infringement: Because the dataset was compiled from unauthorized shadow libraries, authors (such as Margaret Atwood, Stephen King, and Sarah Silverman) never consented or received compensation. [[1], [2], [3], [4]] * Lawsuits: The discovery of Books3 triggered multiple class-action copyright lawsuits against tech companies and AI developers, including legal actions targeting Meta, Bloomberg, and Adobe. [[1], [2], [3]] * Takedowns: Rights groups issued DMCA notices, leading to the removal of components of the dataset from major hosting platforms like Hugging Face and The-Eye. [[1], [2]] Would you like to know how to check if a specific author or book title was included in the Books3 dataset? The Atlantic
